summary:
Terengganu is one of the 13 states of Malaysia and stands under the national framework: sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, with a maximum of 20 years plus whipping. Sodomy has been criminalised in Malaysian law since 1871. These provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens, so a foreign visitor in Terengganu is exposed to them on the same terms as a resident.

The state layer adds a second offence that reaches only Muslims. Every one of the 13 states, Terengganu included, maintains a Sharia enactment criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Enforcement sits with the state Islamic religious department, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing. Litigation has narrowed this layer without loosening the federal one: the Federal Court struck down Selangor's cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, while sections 377A and 377B remain fully intact. A non-Muslim foreign visitor therefore falls outside the Sharia offence but remains squarely covered by the Penal Code.

Official messaging in Terengganu is explicitly hostile. In May 2025 a Terengganu state executive councillor confirmed that warning signboards against homosexual practices installed at strategic locations across the state are intended to instil hatred of homosexual acts, and stated that the state wants people to regard those acts as dirty, wrong and to be avoided. This is state-level endorsement of anti-homosexual signage, and it sets the tone a gender-nonconforming visitor can expect from public authorities in the state.

Civil society has contested the campaign on the record. In May 2025 thirteen organisations including Justice for Sisters urged the Kuala Terengganu City Council to remove the anti-LGBT signboards, describing them as discriminatory and a violation of international human rights law, and criticising the executive councillor's defence of the boards as inciting hatred and discrimination. The pushback has not produced a documented removal.

Enforcement across Malaysia is conducted in public and produces outing as well as prosecution. Raid-based arrest of gender-nonconforming people by religious departments, mass arrests at venues, and lethal violence against trans women with impunity are documented nationally; tourists are rarely targeted individually, but a visitor who is visibly gender-nonconforming in Terengganu faces the same official hostility expressed in the state's signage campaign. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law anywhere in Malaysia.
tangentialFactors:
The hostile messaging in Terengganu sits within a national pattern of state-backed restriction: all 13 states and the federal territories maintain Sharia cross-dressing offences, government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored.

Enforcement elsewhere in Malaysia shows how quickly a hostile climate converts into arrests. In November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Kuala Lumpur and detained 208 men under section 377B, with detainees' identities leaked to media and 31 foreign nationals held; a second sauna raid followed in Penang days later. A comparable dynamic of public exposure, not private-conduct prosecution, is what the Terengganu signage campaign signals.

The civil-society response is organised and named. Thirteen organisations including Justice for Sisters acted jointly in May 2025, and Justice for Sisters has separately mobilised bailors and legal aid during venue raids, which is a resource a visitor could reach only indirectly.

State executive councillors in Terengganu have publicly defended the anti-LGBT signboard programme as deliberate incitement, and the boards are placed at strategic locations throughout the state, so residents encounter them in the course of ordinary movement.

Federal litigation has produced only partial relief: the Federal Court's February 2021 ruling on Selangor and its February 2024 ruling on 16 Kelantan provisions turned on federalism grounds and did not disturb the Penal Code, leaving state-level exposure in Terengganu otherwise unchanged.
outOfScopeNotes:
The May 2025 civil-society request that the Kuala Terengganu City Council remove the signboards is documented, but whether any boards were taken down is unresolved in the sources.

Terengganu's specific Sharia cross-dressing provision, its section number and its recorded enforcement or prosecution history are not sourced here; the state-level figures cited are the national range common to all 13 states.

No documented arrest, raid or prosecution of a foreign visitor for gender nonconformity in Terengganu appears in the inventory, so the visitor-facing assessment rests on the national enforcement pattern and the state's official messaging rather than on a Terengganu-specific case.
